The net result is that 20025 oil consumption is now estimated at 104.8m b/d (that's ~300,000 b/d higher than the last estimate, and ***a huge 1.1m b/d higher*** than where the IEA pegged a year ago 2025 demand).

The changes also mean that the 105.7m b/d of oil consumption that the IEA now anticipates for 2027 is **higher** than the absolute peak oil demand it forecast a year ago (when it said that global oil consumption would peak in 2029 at 105.6m b/d).

OPEC production rose by 1.16 million barrels per day (mb/d) to 19.44 mb/d last month, according to a recent Bloomberg survey. Last week, the eight OPEC+ countries participating in voluntary output cuts announced another production increase for September, effectively completing the unwinding of the voluntary adjustments introduced in April and November 2023.  

The return to these higher production baselines gives several Gulf producers significant room to increase supply further. Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Kuwait alone could potentially raise production by a combined 6.3 mb/d from July levels if they were to move back towards their respective production targets.   

This highlights both the scale of production lost during the past six months and the potential for a sizeable supply rebound once stability returns. However, any recovery is likely to be gradual, with accumulated inventories and storage facilities needing to be drawn down before shut-in production can be restarted and exports normalised.

The monthly oil market reports from OPEC, the EIA and the IEA continue to highlight a massive divergence in 2026 demand growth expectations, with the gap between OPEC on one hand and the two others now exceeding 2 million barrels per day. OPEC remains the clear outlier, still expecting demand to grow by around 0.6 million b/d, while the EIA and IEA have progressively raised their contraction forecasts to around 1.3 million b/d and 1.6 million b/d, respectively.

The widening gap highlights the extraordinary uncertainty surrounding the demand outlook following six months of Middle East supply disruption and elevated energy prices. It also helps explain why crude oil has struggled to sustain a stronger rally despite tight physical conditions: the market is balancing severe near-term supply constraints against growing concerns that high prices and weaker economic activity are already producing a meaningful demand response.

In 2027, the divergence largely disappears as all three forecasters expect global oil demand growth to rebound strongly next year, with their latest estimates clustering around 2.2–2.4 million b/d. This suggests the disagreement is less about the longer-term trajectory of oil consumption and more about the scale and duration of the demand destruction triggered by this year’s supply shock and elevated prices.

Refineries are enjoying exceptionally strong margins amid tightness across refined products, particularly middle distillates such as diesel, jet fuel and heating oil. The squeeze reflects the loss of supply from two critical refining regions: the Middle East, where disrupted crude flows and refinery outages have curtailed exports, and Russia, where Ukrainian attacks continue to constrain refinery runs.

The Middle East matters disproportionately to the distillate market. Before the war, the region accounted for more than 10% of global refining capacity and had developed into a major export-oriented refining hub, supplying 3.3 million barrels per day of refined products in 2025. Gulf refineries also benefit from ready access to medium and heavier sour crude grades that are particularly well suited to complex refineries configured to maximise yields of diesel, jet fuel and other middle distillates.

The loss of these barrels is therefore difficult to replace quickly, especially with Russian refinery runs also curtailed. The IEA has highlighted diesel and jet fuel as particularly vulnerable to an extended loss of Middle Eastern production and exports, given limited spare flexibility elsewhere in the global refining system.

As the charts highlight, the result has been a surge in distillate cracks well above gasoline margins across the US, Europe and Asia, while the NYMEX 3-2-1 crack spread has climbed to exceptionally elevated levels. In short, refiners able to secure crude and maintain high utilisation rates are currently being handsomely rewarded for a global shortage of refining capacity in precisely the part of the barrel the market needs most.

Some of the world's largest refiners include Sinopec, Saudi Aramco, ExxonMobil, Marathon Petroleum and Valero. The latter two, with their significant exposure to the US refining market, have seen their share prices more than double year to date, highlighting the extraordinary improvement in refining economics as global product shortages have driven crack spreads sharply higher.
